findings.claim: The Athenian Thesmophoria lasted five days, while elsewhere it typically lasted three.
findings.truth: At Athens the Thesmophoria lasted three days; the length varied in other places.
findings.evidence: Thesmophoria, Wikipedia, lines 139–140 (fetched): Athens observed it over three days; other places could vary.

findings.claim: We know no individual Pythia by name from the classical period.
findings.truth: Herodotus names the Pythia Aristonike in his account of the Persian invasion.
findings.evidence: Herodotus, Histories 8.140, Project Gutenberg translation, lines 1830–1832 (fetched).

findings.claim: The Pythia sat above a crack in the earth in the inner sanctuary.
findings.truth: Either qualify this as a traditional account, or omit it. Ancient descriptions of the oracle conflict, and the geological explanation involving an opening and vapours remains debated.

findings.claim: Plutarch says Aspasia was prosecuted for impiety and corrupting Athenian women.
findings.truth: The tradition reported in Plutarch is that Hermippus accused Aspasia of impiety and of procuring free-born women for Pericles.
findings.evidence: Aspasia, Wikipedia, lines 224–225 (fetched), summarising Plutarch, Pericles 24.

findings.claim: The lesson teaches Livia, Agrippina the Younger, the Ara Pacis and Tacitus as its central Roman evidence.
findings.truth: OCR J199/12 specifies Cleopatra VII for foreign powerful women and does not prescribe Livia, Agrippina, the Ara Pacis or Tacitus. Rebuild this lesson around Cleopatra and the prescribed sources, or clearly label the extra material as non-exam extension.
findings.evidence: OCR J199 specification, section 2c ‘Women in the Ancient World’: ‘Women to be Feared’ and prescribed-source lists.
findings.ruling: Labelled as extension; Cleopatra named as prescribed. A Cleopatra-centred rebuild of L3 is recorded for Tom.

findings.claim: Camilla is killed from behind while distracted by Chloreus’ armour.
findings.truth: Arruns attacks from an ambush, but his spear strikes Camilla in the breast.
findings.evidence: Virgil, Aeneid 11, Project Gutenberg translation, lines 12196–12205 and 12244–12265 (fetched).

findings.claim: Camilla is killed by a named Roman soldier.
findings.truth: Camilla is killed by Arruns, an Italian warrior in the poem’s pre-Roman setting.
findings.evidence: Virgil, Aeneid 11, Project Gutenberg translation, lines 12196–12205 and 12244–12265 (fetched).

findings.claim: Every ancient text on women was written by a man.
findings.truth: Most surviving texts used for this topic were written by men, but women such as Sappho also wrote surviving ancient poetry.
Fragments attributed to Cornelia survive in manuscripts of Cornelius Nepos, although their authenticity is disputed.
findings.evidence: Cornelia (mother of the Gracchi), Wikipedia, lines 170–184 (fetched).

findings.claim: Neaira is known from a Roman legal text.
findings.truth: Against Neaira is an Athenian court speech, attributed to Demosthenes.
findings.evidence: OCR J199 specification, section 2c: Neaira is listed under Greece; the lesson itself identifies her as an Athenian woman.

findings.claim: The exact English quotation attributed to the Ampharete Stele.
findings.truth: This may be a valid translation, but its wording was not verifiable against a fetched primary or museum source in this check.
findings.evidence: No reachable fetched source for the Ampharete inscription’s English translation.

summary: Five lessons checked. Eight findings have surgical factual fixes; two broader source or scope concerns are left for adjudication.
